Worked example · distribution

Three godowns and one stock figure.

A trading and distribution walkthrough, to sit beside the interiors one. Same product, a completely different week: stock in three places, credit given to contractors on trust, and an input tax credit claim nobody checked against GSTR-2B before it was filed.

Invented, and better said in the first line than buried. There is no distributor here at all — this is assembled from the trading businesses we have scoped and built for, with the numbers made up and the shapes real. Every figure below is illustrative and labelled so. When a real distributor is willing to be named, their name goes here and this paragraph goes.

The business

Fifty-five people. A main warehouse on the outskirts and two branch godowns forty and ninety kilometres out, each with its own staff and its own delivery vehicles. They sell cement, TMT bar, AAC block, PVC and CPVC pipe and a range of electricals — switchgear, wire, fittings — to two very different customers: contractors who buy by the load on thirty to sixty days of credit, and retailers who buy smaller and pay faster.

Around four hundred order lines a week, seven suppliers who matter and a long tail who do not, and a margin thin enough that one mis-stated tax credit is a real month. They are not in trouble. They are in the position that makes a systems project worth doing: growing, profitable, and running on arrangements that worked at half this size.

Where the week went before

Nothing dramatic. Four ordinary habits, each of which made sense when there was one godown and thirty people.

  • Stock was counted on Saturdays. Three people, half a day, three locations, and by Tuesday afternoon the number was a memory of Saturday rather than a fact.
  • Orders were promised against numbers nobody trusted. A salesman rang the godown, the godown said probably, and roughly one load in nine went out short or went out and came back.
  • Input tax credit was claimed off the purchase register, because that is what was in front of them. Nobody matched it to GSTR-2B first, so credit for suppliers who had not filed was claimed and then written back later, with interest.
  • Receivables were chased from memory. Two people knew who was overdue. Both were usually right and neither could produce a list, and a contractor who had gone past ninety days could still collect a fresh load because the godown had no reason to ask.
  • And branch pricing was whatever the printed rate card said, revised whenever somebody remembered, which meant the same contractor was quoted two prices in one week by two branches and noticed.

What changed, in what order

Four phases across about seven months. The ordering was argued about and this is where it landed.

  1. Phase one: the item master, before anything else

    Not a module. Six weeks of unglamorous work reducing about 2,900 item rows to roughly 1,100 real items with one code, one unit of measure and one conversion factor each. Cement in bags with a bag-to-tonne factor, TMT in tonnes with a per-piece weight by size, pipe in metres. Nothing else could start until this was settled, because every subsequent number is built on it.

  2. Phase two: stock across three locations

    One ledger with three stock locations and transfers between them recorded as movements rather than as a phone call. Availability became a live figure per location, with quantity reserved against confirmed orders subtracted from it. The Saturday count did not disappear — it became a monthly reconciliation against a figure the system already claimed, which is a different and much shorter job.

  3. Phase three: order to dispatch to invoice

    An order confirms against available stock, a delivery challan is raised against specific order lines with vehicle and driver, and the database refuses to dispatch more than the line ordered instead of letting somebody fix it later. The invoice is raised from what actually left the godown. E-way bill numbers are recorded on the challan; they are still generated by a person on the NIC portal, and IRNs are still raised on the government portal exactly as before. Ordence does neither, and that was said in the scope.

  4. Phase four: purchase, GSTR-2B and the receivables ledger

    Purchase invoices matched against GSTR-2B line by line, with the unmatched ones shown as a list of supplier names rather than a total. Ageing across five buckets computed from the ledger instead of remembered, credit limits attached to customers, and an order for a contractor past his limit held for a named person to release rather than blocked by an argument at the gate.

What was hard, and we are not going to soften it

The item master was the whole project for six weeks and nobody enjoyed it. Nine years of rows had TMT 12mm, 12 MM TMT and Fe500D 12 as three separate items with three separate stock balances, cement recorded sometimes by brand and sometimes by grade, and AAC block in three sizes under one code. There is no clever import that solves this. Somebody who knows the products has to sit down and say these two are the same and that third one is not, and that person was needed by the business for other things. We would rather delay a go-live than load a clean system with dirty data, because the result of the second is an expensive spreadsheet.

The branch staff preferred the phone, and they were not being difficult. A call took eleven seconds and got a human answer; the first stock screen took four taps on a mid-range Android in a godown with one bar of signal. Training did not fix that and would not have. Cutting the screen to one search box and a number, and making it work on a bad connection, did. By about week seven the calls had mostly stopped, because looking was faster than ringing.

One module was scoped, priced and then dropped: bin-location scanning in the godowns. It reads well on paper and it is genuinely useful in a warehouse of small parts. This is a warehouse where cement moves by the truckload and TMT is picked with a crane, and the only stock it would have helped with was electricals — about four percent of value. We took it out of the scope and the price at the pilot, which is the cheapest place to find that out.

And one thing did not get better. Collections still depend on somebody phoning a contractor and asking. The system produces the list, the ageing and the evidence, and it will not make the call. Any vendor implying otherwise is selling you software that does not exist.

What it did not touch

The statutory books stayed in Tally, on purpose, exported with identifiers that update rather than duplicate on a re-run. Their CA files the returns, as before. Ordence prepares and evidences — an ITC register in the shape GSTR-3B Table 4 wants, a sales register in the shape GSTR-1 wants — and nothing is submitted to GSTN by us, because we do not do that and do not want the portal credentials.

There was also no big-bang Monday. Phase two ran at the main warehouse for three weeks before either branch saw it, and the second branch went last on purpose because its manager was the most sceptical and the most listened-to. Convincing him with a working system was worth more than convincing him with a plan.

Your godowns are not these godowns.

But if the Saturday count and the probably on the phone sound familiar, that is the conversation. Tell us how many locations you have and what your item master looks like on a bad day.
